title: English — Grade 6 Entrance
subject: english
instructions:
Cambridge Lower Secondary Placement Test — Stage 6, English Paper 1.

- Answer **all** questions.
- Write your answer to each question in the space provided.
- You should pay attention to punctuation, spelling and handwriting.

The total mark for this paper is 50. The number of marks for each question or part question is shown in brackets [ ]. Suggestions for how long to spend on each section are given in the booklet.

sections.title: Section A: Reading — Text A
sections.instructions: Spend 30 minutes on Section A (Reading) in total. Read **Text A** and answer questions 1–6.
sections.passage:
# Hanging on (no threads allowed!)

*(Paragraph 1, lines 1–3)* El Capitan is a vertical rock formation in Yosemite National Park, USA. This monster of exposed granite stretches for about 900 metres from base to summit, providing the ultimate challenge for rock climbers.

*(Paragraph 2, lines 4–7)* On 27 December 2014, after years of preparation, Tommy Caldwell and Kevin Jorgeson set out to climb the Dawn Wall, so called because it is the first part of El Capitan to get sunlight from the east. This climb is considered El Capitan's most treacherous route and one of the hardest climbs in the world.

*(Paragraph 3, lines 8–14)* To climb huge rock faces such as El Capitan, mountaineering equipment is usually needed. A climber hammers pegs into small cracks in the rock face. Nylon rungs, like steps on a ladder, are then clipped into place and the climber moves up the rungs far enough to repeat the process. However, free climbers do not use any equipment, using nothing more than hands and feet to progress upwards. Caldwell and Jorgeson joined forces in 2009 to map a free climb route up the Dawn Wall. Free climbing the Dawn Wall had never been done before – it had always been considered impossible.

*(Paragraph 4, lines 15–23)* The climb involved slippery footholds, the men relying only on the friction of their rubber-soled shoes against the rocks to prevent them from falling. They were forced to hang on by their fingertips to tiny razor-sharp edges protruding from the smooth rock. One section of the climb, which they referred to as Pitch 15, almost defeated Jorgeson. This is a lengthy, sideways traverse*, which is the most challenging section as there is almost nothing to cling onto. However, Jorgeson was determined not to abandon the venture and Caldwell refused to continue alone. So, they carried on together. On 14 January 2015, after 19 days on the sheer rock face, Caldwell and Jorgeson hauled themselves over the upper lip of the Dawn Wall and into the history books.

**Glossary** — *a traverse*: a route on the side of a rock or cliff

sections.title: Section A: Reading — Text B
sections.passage:
*(Paragraph 1, lines 1–3)* Rock climbing can take you to amazing and unimaginable places. It will inspire you to do things that others may think are impossible to achieve and it will, in all probability, change your whole outlook on life.

*(Paragraph 2, lines 4–14)* The perfect way to begin is by heading out with friends who already know how it's done. But actually, for most people that isn't a possibility. I remember sitting alone in my climbing harness, hanging on a rope about five metres above the ground, thinking, 'Why can't I go up any further?' This was my debut to climbing on natural rock. I hadn't even tried climbing on an indoor wall prior to that trip. It may well be wise for you to do this before venturing outside. Many towns and cities have indoor climbing walls these days, and they're easy to find with a quick search on the internet. Wall climbing is great fun, however good or bad you are at it, but if you do want to go outdoors straightaway there's no reason you shouldn't. But at least get the basics right first. You can do this by: starting on lower-level slopes without a harness, making yourself familiar with the rock face, and getting used to walking in climbing shoes – they can feel quite different from your ordinary trainers.

*(Paragraph 3, lines 15–21)* New climbers tend to try to move directly upwards, when they should be thinking about moving sideways or even stepping down when necessary. The important thing is to always maintain three points of contact with the rock (for example, two feet and one hand), and when you feel confident enough, try leaning slightly away from it so you have a clear view of where to put your feet next. If you do decide to invest in kit, the essentials are a helmet, harness and rope. If you're intending to explore a new region, a local climbing guide is also a must. They will have details of climbs of all difficulties and will advise on the most appropriate climb for you.

questions.prompt:
Give **one** word and **one** phrase from the first paragraph (lines 1–3) that tell the reader that climbing El Capitan is not easy.

word: ______

phrase: ______
questions.answerKey: word: monster; phrase: (providing) the ultimate challenge

questions.prompt:
Look at the second paragraph (lines 4–7).

How did the 'Dawn Wall' get its name?
questions.answerKey: Because it is the first part of El Capitan to get sunlight from the east (i.e. at dawn).

questions.prompt:
Look at the second paragraph (lines 4–7).

Give **one** word that means *dangerous*.

Look at the third paragraph (lines 8–14).

Give **one** word that introduces a contrasting idea.

Look at the third paragraph (lines 8–14).

Give **one** phrase that means *only*.

Look at the third paragraph (lines 8–14).

Give **one** two-word phrase that tells the reader Caldwell and Jorgeson worked together.

Give **two** examples of a passive verb form from the third paragraph. Give **one** example using a present verb form and **one** example using a past verb form.

present passive: ______

past passive: ______
questions.answerKey: present passive: 'is (usually) needed' or 'are (then) clipped (into place)'; past passive: 'had (never) been done' or 'had (always) been considered'

questions.prompt:
Look at the fourth paragraph (lines 15–23).

Explain in your own words what makes the Dawn Wall such a difficult climb. Give **one** quotation from the text to support your answer.

Explanation: ______

Quotation: ______
questions.criteria:
1 point: explanation in the student's own words of what makes the climb difficult (e.g. the rock is smooth/slippery with almost nothing to hold onto; climbers must rely on friction and cling by their fingertips to tiny sharp edges).
1 point: a relevant supporting quotation from paragraph 4, e.g. 'slippery footholds', 'hang on by their fingertips to tiny razor-sharp edges', 'there is almost nothing to cling onto'.
Do not award the explanation point if it merely repeats the quotation word for word.

questions.prompt:
Look at the fourth paragraph (lines 15–23).

After completing the challenge Caldwell and Jorgeson became famous.

Give **one** phrase from the text that tells the reader this.

Look at the heading, 'Hanging on (no threads allowed!)'.

Why do you think this heading is suitable for this text? Give **two** ideas.
questions.criteria: 1 point per valid idea, max 2. Acceptable ideas include: the climbers literally had to hang on (by their fingertips) to the rock; 'no threads allowed' refers to free climbing without ropes or equipment; it plays on the saying 'hanging on by a thread', suggesting danger; it is a joke/pun that catches the reader's attention.

questions.prompt:

A. The text has numbered points.
B. The text has an introductory paragraph.
C. The text is non-chronologically organised.
D. The text uses one-sentence paragraphs.
E. The text uses time connectives.
What is the purpose of **Text B**? Choose **one** option.
Give **one** word from the second paragraph (lines 4–14) that introduces a contrasting and surprising idea.

Look at line 12 in **Text B** ('You can do this by: starting on lower-level slopes without a harness, ...'). Why has a colon ( : ) been used?

Give **one** reason.
questions.answerKey: To introduce a list (of ways to get the basics right).

questions.prompt:
Why has a dash ( – ) been used in line 13 of **Text B** ('...getting used to walking in climbing shoes – they can feel quite different from your ordinary trainers')?

Give **one** reason.
questions.answerKey: To add extra information / an explanatory comment (about climbing shoes).

questions.prompt:
Your friend wants to take up rock climbing and has asked you what they should do.

Write a list of tips using the information from **Text B**. (Write each tip on its own line as a bullet point.)
questions.criteria:
1 point per correct tip drawn from Text B, max 3. Acceptable tips include: go climbing with (experienced) friends who know how it's done; try an indoor climbing wall first; start on lower-level slopes without a harness; get familiar with the rock face; get used to walking in climbing shoes; don't only move upwards — move sideways or step down when necessary; always keep three points of contact with the rock; lean slightly away from the rock to see where to put your feet; buy the essential kit (helmet, harness, rope); use a local climbing guide when exploring a new region.
Answers must be presented as a list of tips based on Text B.

questions.prompt: Write a summary of up to 50 words about what to do before taking up rock climbing seriously. Include **four** points from your list (question 10(a)). Use your own words as far as possible.
questions.criteria:
2 points: a coherent summary of no more than about 50 words containing four distinct valid points from Text B, expressed mostly in the student's own words.
1 point: a summary with only two or three valid points, or one that noticeably exceeds the word limit or copies heavily from the text.
0 points: fewer than two valid points.

questions.prompt:
Write an account for your friend about a new activity that you have tried.

Think about:

- the type of activity
- what you need for the activity
- persuading your friend why it is a good activity
- any helpful tips.

(You may plan your account first, but only your final written account will be marked.)
questions.criteria:
Content and purpose (up to 10): a clear, engaging account addressed to a friend about a new activity the writer has tried; covers the type of activity, what is needed for it, persuades the friend that it is a good activity, and offers helpful tips.
Organisation (up to 5): logical structure with paragraphs, an effective opening and ending, and an appropriate friendly/informal register.
Style and vocabulary (up to 5): varied sentence structures and a good range of descriptive and persuasive language.
Accuracy (up to 5): correct spelling, punctuation and grammar.

importNotes: Q6 (tick two boxes) adapted to lettered short_answer with key 'B and E' — variant student formats like 'E and B' or 'B, E' rely on AI near-miss checking; teacher may want to confirm marking behaves as expected

Grading criteria for the 25-mark writing task (Q11) and other open_response questions were written by the parser, not taken from an official Cambridge mark scheme — teacher should review the rubric split (10/5/5/5)

Source Q6 is a tick-TWO-boxes task; the schema's single correctChoiceId cannot encode two answers, so it was adapted into a short_answer with lettered options A–E and answerKey 'B and E' (introductory paragraph + time connectives) — teacher should verify.

Q9(a)/(b) refer to printed line numbers in Text B, which do not survive digital reflow; the relevant quotations were added in brackets to the prompts, and paragraph/line-range markers were added to both passages.
Section A was split into two sections (Text A / Text B) so each reading passage attaches to its questions; the 30-minute suggestion covers both.

No official mark scheme in the source: all short-answer keys were derived from the texts (e.g. 'monster'/'the ultimate challenge', 'treacherous', 'However', 'nothing more than', 'joined forces', 'actually') and should be reviewed, especially Q1 and Q3(d) where multiple valid quotes exist.
Q11 (writing, 25 marks) has no rubric in the source; the 10/5/5/5 criteria breakdown was written following Cambridge account-writing conventions.
The 'Space for your plan' box for Q11 was noted in the prompt as unmarked planning; blank lined pages 7–8 of the PDF were skipped.
